resources.string: Tap Connect to join the Yggdrasil network
One URI per line: tls://, quic://, tcp://, ws://, wss://
Reconnect to apply the new peers
No server yet. The app logs in over SSH and sets up Yggdrasil and WireGuard on it by itself.
WireGuard: port %1$d · your IP %2$s · server peers: %3$d · IPv6 internet: %4$s
Forget this server in the app? Nothing is changed on the server itself.

Ubuntu or Debian with root (or passwordless sudo). The app installs yggdrasil and wireguard-tools, sets up NAT and closes everything on the Yggdrasil interface except WireGuard, SSH and ping. Safe to run again.
Key saved — paste a new one to replace it
Saved — leave empty to keep it
Not set up yet — the details are saved, tap Set up to try again
None — all apps go through the VPN
Checked apps use the regular internet, without the VPN (banks, local services). Applied on reconnect.
Scan with the camera of the other phone (with YggTunnel installed) or send the link — the profile opens in YggTunnel.
Whoever has this code can use your server. Share it only with your own devices.
Paste the yggtunnel://import#… link from the other phone.
No profile found in this text
Use the server %1$s from this profile?
Add the server %1$s from this profile and make it active? The current servers stay in the list.
WireGuard: port %1$d · your IP %2$s · IPv6 internet: %3$s
Devices on the server: %1$d. Tap one for actions.
This is the profile of this phone: on another device the same key works only while this phone is off the tunnel (a new phone instead of this one). For a second device use Add.
The device is disconnected at once and can no longer use the server. To bring it back, add it again and import the new profile on it.
This is this phone: the tunnel stops working here until you set the server up again (Set up again).
Only the checked apps use the VPN, all others go to the regular internet. Nothing checked — all apps use the VPN. Applied on reconnect.
Start on boot, block traffic without the VPN

Android starts YggTunnel by itself after a reboot or a crash when it is the always-on VPN.

In the settings: tap ⚙ next to YggTunnel → turn on “Always-on VPN”. “Block connections without VPN” is a kill switch: while the tunnel is down, apps have no internet at all (apps chosen to bypass the VPN lose it too).

A Quick Settings tile is also available: edit the tiles in the notification shade and add YggTunnel.
%1$d fast peers from the catalog — Save to use them
Edited by hand — not refreshed automatically. Catalog makes it automatic again.
From the catalog (%1$s), refreshed weekly by itself.
Built-in list; refreshed from the catalog by itself after connecting.

Yggdrasil peering inside HTTPS to your own site on this server: to the network it is ordinary traffic to the site with its real certificate. Needs a WebSocket location in the site’s web server pointing to Yggdrasil’s ws://127.0.0.1 listener. The peer is pinned and kept first.

The app finds the HTTPS site in nginx on your server (also behind telemt, xray, haproxy on 443) and adds a secret path to it, or creates a site with a free Let’s Encrypt certificate when 443 is free. Every changed file is backed up, any error rolls everything back.
Or enter the address by hand:
Take the wrapper off the server (the location in nginx and Yggdrasil’s local listener)? “Forget only” just removes the address from the app.

There is no HTTPS site on the server yet, and ports 443 and 80 are free: the app will install nginx, get a Let’s Encrypt certificate and make a small site.\n\nYou need a domain whose DNS A record points to %1$s. A free one is fine: deSEC (dedyn.io), DuckDNS, FreeDNS.

telemt passes non-Telegram traffic on to the site, but cuts such connections after 5 s of silence, 60 s in total or 5 MB — enough for a web page, not for a tunnel (the wss peer would drop every few seconds).\n\nThe app can raise these limits in /etc/telemt/telemt.toml: 5 min of silence, a day, no byte cap. telemt restarts (Telegram clients reconnect within seconds); the config is backed up. Port scanners may then hold a connection longer.

Disconnected — the VPN is off. Connecting… — the Yggdrasil node is looking for peers (or waits for the WireGuard handshake with the server). Connected — there are live peers; “via server” — all traffic goes through your server. Below: your Yggdrasil address, live peers, routes, uptime and the tunnel state.
The permanent address of this phone in the Yggdrasil network (200::/7), made from the node key. Tap to copy — other Yggdrasil nodes can reach the phone by it.
Starts the VPN: the Yggdrasil node and, with a set-up server, the WireGuard tunnel through it. Android asks for the VPN permission the first time. Only one VPN can run at a time.

Your own server: the app sets it up over SSH (Yggdrasil, WireGuard, NAT) and then sends all traffic through it. The phone reaches the server through the Yggdrasil network, not directly, so the tunnel does not depend on a direct connection to the server’s address.
Enter the IP, SSH port, user and private key — the app installs and configures everything on Ubuntu/Debian by itself and shows the log.
A profile from another phone (a yggtunnel://import#… link or QR code): a ready connection to that server, no SSH access needed.
The phone finds the server inside Yggdrasil by this address. Tap to copy.

The WireGuard port on the server, your address inside the tunnel, how many Yggdrasil peers the server had at setup, and whether it has IPv6 internet (if not, IPv6 on the phone is blocked so nothing leaks past the tunnel).
Yggdrasil peering inside HTTPS to your own site on the server, on the usual port 443. Tap to set it up automatically, enter the address by hand or remove it.
On — all of the phone’s internet goes through the server (sites see its IP). Off — the VPN only gives access to the Yggdrasil network, everything else goes as usual. Applied on reconnect.
Runs the server setup over SSH once more: packages, configs, the server’s peers. Keys and devices are kept; safe to run any number of times.
Forgets the server in the app. Nothing is changed on the server itself.
Every device with access to the server: names, when they were online, traffic. Add a new one (QR code), rename, remove or show a profile again.

Yggdrasil nodes the phone joins the network through. ● connected (latency, ↓ received, ↑ sent), ◌ error, ○ not tried yet, ◇ kept in reserve by auto-pick. “Not in the list” — a link that is no longer listed (until reconnect).
The list of peer addresses: tls://, quic://, tcp://, ws://, wss://. Catalog picks fast reliable peers from the public catalog. Changes apply on reconnect.

Half a minute after connecting, keeps the chosen number of the fastest peers (plus your server’s own) and parks the rest in reserve; if fewer than 2 stay alive, the reserve is dialed again. 3 is a good balance of reliability and battery.
Bypass — the checked apps go around the VPN (banks, local services). Only through VPN — only the checked apps use it. Applied on reconnect.
An Android system setting: the VPN starts by itself after a reboot, and “Block connections without VPN” lets no traffic out while the tunnel is down.
The latest messages of the Yggdrasil node and the tunnel — useful when something does not connect. Can be copied.
Loads public peers from publicpeers.neilalexander.dev, keeps the reliable ones (up in ≥ 90% of checks), times them from the phone and picks the fastest.
Creates a key for a new device, registers it on the server and shows a QR code and a link to import.
Asks the server again for the device list and their state.
Tap for actions: rename, show the QR code and link, copy the public key, remove. Green dot — handshake within the last 3 minutes.
Sends the profile link through a messenger; on the other phone it opens in YggTunnel.

The key you log in to the server with (OpenSSH or PEM text). It stays in the app’s private storage and is used only to set the server up. Choose key file reads it from a file, Termux’s home folder included.
The port your server’s SSH listens on (22 unless you changed it).
root, or a user with passwordless sudo — setup installs packages and changes system configs.
Hold any button or item to see what it does.

For screenshots and showing the screen: every address — yours and public ones, IPs, domains, peer URIs, the wss path, device names — is covered with a grainy blur. Under the grain is a random string, not the address, so nothing can be read out of a screenshot. Tapping still copies the real address.

Peers, all traffic through the server, auto-pick, app lists, the wrapper, a new or imported server — the running VPN takes such changes only on reconnect. On: it reconnects by itself a second after the last change (a short break). Off: you reconnect when convenient.
Colour theme and transparency, as in AppShelf. Changes at once, the window stays open.
Translucent cards and dialogs over the soft colour background. Off — solid surfaces, a bit easier to read in the sun.
Off — all listed peers stay connected

How many of the fastest peers stay connected (your server’s own peers are always kept on top). Yggdrasil sends your traffic along one path, so more peers do not make it faster — each extra link costs battery, keepalive traffic and routing updates. 2 — the most economical, 3 — the balance: one can fail and two remain, 4–5 — for unstable networks or when public peers often go down. More than 5 is rarely useful on a phone.
Unrestricted — Android leaves the VPN alone

Android optimises the app’s battery use: on some phones (MIUI / HyperOS especially) it may pause or slow the VPN in the background, and the tunnel drops.\n\nAllow — the system asks to let YggTunnel run without restrictions. If the phone has its own battery saver, App settings → Battery → Unrestricted. A VPN that is idle uses almost no battery.
YggTunnel may run in the background without restrictions — Android will not pause the VPN. On MIUI / HyperOS also check App settings → Battery.
Whether Android may limit the app in the background to save battery. For a VPN it should be Unrestricted, otherwise the tunnel can drop while the screen is off.

A small pill at the camera cutout that appears when the connection changes: connecting, connected, off, failed. Over other apps it needs the «Display over other apps» permission (the settings screen opens when you turn it on); without it, it shows only while this app is open.
How far below the top edge of the screen the island sits, in % of the screen height. Each step shows the island at the new place. Raise or lower it until the camera does not cover the text.
A notification with the status and Disconnect while connected. Off by default: the Quick Settings tile does the same, and Android keeps a running VPN alive and shows the key icon by itself.
A password-protected file — for a new phone or a reinstall

Everything in one file: the server and its SSH key, the VPN keys (the phone keeps its Yggdrasil address), devices, peers and all settings. It is encrypted with your password — without it the file is useless. Android’s own backups are off for this app on purpose.
There is no way to recover a forgotten password — keep it somewhere safe.
The current settings will be replaced after you confirm.
This is not a YggTunnel backup file
Wrong password, or the file is damaged
Backup of %1$s, server: %2$s.\n\nReplace all current settings with it?
Saves all settings with keys to a password-protected file, or restores them. Use it before moving to a new phone or reinstalling.
Encrypts all settings with your password (PBKDF2 + AES-256-GCM) and lets you choose where to save the file.
Opens a backup file, checks the password and shows what is inside before replacing anything.
%1$d of %2$d · tap to switch or add another

You can keep several servers and switch between them: the active one carries the tunnel, its own peers (direct and wss) are put first in the peer list. Add another one over SSH or import a profile. «Edit» next to a server changes its SSH details; the saved key is never shown.
A reboot is required to finish earlier updates
Runs apt update and apt upgrade on the server. Services may restart for a moment (the tunnel too); configuration files you changed are kept.
The state of the server over SSH, read-only: CPU, memory, disk, network, services, Yggdrasil and WireGuard, pending updates. Refreshes every 15 seconds while open.
Install the pending package updates (apt upgrade) after a confirmation, with a log.
Our server\'s peers (tls, quic, wss) are always used, first — even if removed here (Peers → Always use our server\'s peers).
Opening the app connects at once, as if you pressed Connect. Not when it is opened by a profile link or after a crash. To keep the VPN on without opening the app use Always-on VPN.

The active server\'s own peers — direct TLS, QUIC on the same port and the wss wrapper through its site — are always in the peer list, first, and auto-pick never parks them. Off: the list is exactly what you saved.
Speed of the best by ping
Each one: connecting, ping and loss to your server through that peer; then the speed of the best by ping.
No server set up: only connecting and the link\'s latency.
Done: %1$d of %2$d connected. The best are ticked — tick others if you like, then Use.

Downloads the whole public peer list and tests the ones you choose from this phone: each through a separate temporary node, so the running connection is not touched. Ticked peers become your list; our server\'s own peers stay in front.
tls, quic and wss are encrypted; tcp and ws carry only Yggdrasil\'s own encryption.
Only peers that answered at least 90% of the public list\'s hourly checks.

Every chosen peer is connected and pinged, 24 at once. Then the speed is measured only for this many with the fewest losses and the lowest ping — one at a time, so the measurements do not share your line. Saves time and the server\'s traffic.
How many of the best are ticked after the test. Auto-pick (below in Peers) then keeps the fastest few of them connected.
Makes the ticked peers your peer list, best first. The weekly catalog refresh will not replace it.
While connected, checks every few seconds: 8.8.8.8 through the tunnel, your server through Yggdrasil and the server\'s public address directly. Drops and their length are marked.
Nothing yet — the log fills while connected.

Pings while connected, to see when and where the connection dropped: 8.8.8.8 through the tunnel (the internet through your server), the server over Yggdrasil (the Yggdrasil path) and its public address outside the VPN (the direct path). Kept on the phone only, about 2 MB.
Install the speed test on the server

Puts a tiny UDP sender on the server, reachable only at its Yggdrasil address and only with a secret the app keeps; at most 1 GB a day. Each measurement downloads 2 MB from the server — it counts towards the server\'s traffic.
The real speed needs the speed test on your server.
Speed: %1$d × %2$d MB ≈ %3$d MB of the server\'s traffic (the server allows %4$d MB a day)
The speed test is not installed on the server
Speed to the phone through Yggdrasil: %1$.1f Mbit/s (average with the ramp-up %2$.1f), %3$.1f MB
Downloads 2 MB from the server\'s speed test through Yggdrasil — the path the tunnel takes — and writes the result into the log. Only when you press it.
A plain copy on the server %s (/etc/yggtunnel/clients, root only) — without SSH keys. Restoring it keeps the SSH keys this phone has.
No saved settings on the server yet

The settings as plain JSON on your server, one file per phone: peers, apps, theme, Yggdrasil and WireGuard keys, servers without their SSH keys. Not encrypted — it is protected only by the server\'s root access. The server also keeps its own description in /etc/yggtunnel/server.json.
Public peers only as a fallback

While a direct link to your server (tls, quic or wss) is up, public peers are parked: otherwise Yggdrasil may send your downloads from the server the long way through them (it prefers low-latency links), slower and through other people\'s nodes. When the direct link is lost they connect again within about 5–15 s.
Update the speed test on the server
The server has the old speed test (it measured only losses) — update it: Peers → Pick
The server has the old speed test: it sent at full speed and measured mostly losses. Update it.

All three links to your server stay up; the traffic goes over the chosen one, the others take over when it is down. QUIC is UDP and avoids TCP inside TCP, but on some networks UDP is much slower — measure after switching.
Which of the server\'s own peers carries the traffic: Yggdrasil sends over the link with the lowest priority, and the server follows it. Measure with Speedtest after switching.
Speed of the best by ping: %1$d of %2$d
Ping and speed through public peers, the best go into the list

Records the state of the link to the server once a second for 2 minutes (the phone kernel\'s TCP: window, threshold, losses, round trip, speed). Tap Record, then run a speed test. The log is sent to your server (/etc/yggtunnel/diag/).
Congestion control of the current link

The algorithm the phone\'s kernel uses to send over the link to the server. westwood is the system default; reno is for comparison. Applies to the current link only — a reconnect brings back the default.
Two minutes of the link\'s TCP state, once a second, plus WireGuard traffic. Run Speedtest meanwhile — the log shows where the upload gets stuck.
Diagnostics saved on the phone, not sent: %s
Diagnostics saved on the phone (no SSH access to the server)

How much not-yet-sent data the phone\'s kernel may hold for the link. Without a limit it grows to megabytes — seconds of delay for everything in the tunnel under load. 128 KB is the default; «no limit» is for comparison, until the app restarts.

The whole tunnel rides one TCP connection to the server. On a lossy mobile uplink such a connection halves its speed at every loss and grows back slowly, so the upload stays far below what the line can do. With several links the phone runs extra Yggdrasil nodes, each with its own TLS connection, and sends through the least busy one. Experimental: compare the upload with 1 and with 3–4. Uses the direct TLS link to your server.
How many TCP connections to your server carry the tunnel. More connections recover from losses faster, which helps the upload on mobile networks. Changes apply on reconnect.
The app hung (no answer for 5 s): report hang-%s saved

When the tunnel stalls or something misbehaves: sends what every part of the app is doing right now (thread and goroutine stacks), the node\'s state and the logs to your server, so the cause can be found. Hangs of the screen are reported by themselves.
SSH: the server\u2019s own address did not answer, connected through Yggdrasil
SSH: the server\u2019s own address did not answer, and the VPN is off (no way through Yggdrasil)
SSH: the server\u2019s own address did not answer; through Yggdrasil too: %s
No checks for %d s (the phone slept or the system paused the app)
The previous session ended without «VPN off»: the app was updated, the system closed it, or it crashed
VPN on (through the server, link %1$s, links: %2$d)
Whether to keep the log and how often to check.
A speed measurement to your server, the upload diagnostics (the link\'s TCP state for 2 minutes) and a problem report — all go to your server.

deSEC (desec.io) is a free DNS service with names like myvpn.dedyn.io. With your deSEC API token the server registers the name, points it to itself and the site is set up right after. The token is kept encrypted on this phone.

The server will create the name and its A record → %1$s, then set the site up (waiting until the name works).
1. Register at desec.io (free) and create an API token under Token management. 2. Paste the token below and choose a name: a new one like myvpn.dedyn.io, or one under a domain you already have there (vpn.yourname.dedyn.io).
saved — leave empty to use it
The server is talking to deSEC…

By password — what a new VPS usually comes with: after the setup the app adds its own SSH key to the server and logs in with it from then on (for root the password is not kept). By SSH key — if you already have one.
After the setup the app adds its own SSH key to the server and uses it instead. For a user other than root the password is kept (encrypted) for sudo.
One more step — answer in the next window
